It's been raining like crazy here the last two months. We've even had some snow. This makes the roads really wet and gritty, and even with a set of full size fenders, this can cause a lot of crap to get thrown up onto your shoes, drivetrain, the bottom bracket, and the underside of your bike where your derailleur cables are. You need a mudflap. Those cost money, and many shops don't even stock them, so you'll either have to order it or make your own.

The good news is that if you've got some duct tape and an old coat hanger, you can make your own flap for free in about 20 minutes or less. I used black duct tape for mine. You can use any color of duct tape you want.

Start by cleaning off the inside and outside of the bottom of your front fender/mudguard. This is to make sure the tape has a clean surface to adhere to. Then cut yourself a length of tape that can reach from at least one inch above the bottom of the fender all the way down to an inch and a half to two inches off the ground. Use your best judgement for how far down it should go, and don't worry about it being floppy. The coat hanger will make the flap nice and rigid by the time you're done.

Take your length of tape and attach one end to the inside of the fender at an angle that makes it stick out diagonally from the side of the bicycle. Then take an equal length of tape and cover the sticky side of the previous piece starting from the outside of the bottom of the fender. Don't worry about making it perfect. You can trim the tape with scissors later or simply fold another piece over the edge to make it clean looking. Now do the other side of the fender exactly the same way. Then fill in the center with another 2 strips or more, depending on how wide your fender is. You should now have the basic outline of your mudflap done, and it should be shaped like an elongated trapezoid.

Next measure the bottom of your flap and cut yourself a straight piece of coat hanger that is a few centimeters less than this length. If you don't have wire cutters, you can simply bend a point on the coat hanger back and forth until it snaps apart. Once you have your straight piece for the bottom, cut yourself a piece of tape slightly larger than the bottom of the flap. Adhere one half of this strip horizontally along the bottom of the flap, place the wire in the center of it like a hotdog, then fold the other half of the tape to stick over to the opposite side of the flap. Trim the outside edges of the tape if they are sticking out. Now that the wire is taped in, you can shape the mudflap by gently bending the wire! Do this now. Shape the wire so that the bottom of the mudflap is slightly curving in around the tire towards the front of the bike. Now measure the flap from top to bottom and cut yourself another piece of wire from the coat hanger to go from about a half inch on the fender almost all the way down to the bottom of the flap. Tape that vertically to the center of the inside of the flap and bend it so it slightly curves towards the tire.

Take your scissors and trim any odd bits of tape sticking out. Add some folded over pieces of tape around the outside edges at this point if you want. This is optional but recommended, since it helps give the flap a cleaner look and can balance out the shape of the flap if you made it lopsided. Lastly, wrap a piece of tape or two around the bottom of the fender horizontally to give it a nice clean look and help keep the flap well adhered to the fender.

You're done. You should now have a nice rigid light weight durable mudflap, and you didn't need to drill holes in your fender to install it! Best of all, if you did it right and used an appropriate duct tape color, it probably looks good too. No silly milk jugs or coke bottles with zip ties for you! When it comes time to replace the flap, as all flaps eventually wear out, you can probably re-use the same 2 pieces of wire hanger.

Enjoy! If you did this, let me know whether you like it or not.

Email, and by convenient I also mean secure. I don't use a free email provider, I instead use my own domain with MX records pointing to a paid email host that respects my privacy. And if for some reason I want to switch, I just update the MX records and copy my emails to the new provider. Instead if I were using free hosting I would have to either forward from oldemail@free-email-provider.tld (old provider still sees the emails) or change the email addresses I use on everything to the new provider (something that isn't possible on some websites). Having my own domain is also useful as I can send an email to anything@mydomain.tld and it gets sent to my email provider. So I could have voat@mydomain.tld and eff@mydomain.tld. And if the EFF had an email breach and that email was then used to target spam to, I could see that it was the EFF that leaked the email as all the spam is sent to eff@mydomain.tld, not that the EFF are likely to have a breach.

Back in 2008, I inherited my first computer - an old piece of junk with 128MB ram, 8GB harddrive and god knows what version of intel celeron CPU. The only OS that I could use on it to gain any performance at all was FreeBSD.

Compared to that, your laptop looks like a dream. (I blame windows for making you believe your laptop is underpowered - it is more than sufficient for most of your daily tasks, and it is even good enough for computationally heavy research in some ways).

The others here are all correct - there is no "right" distro for your laptop. Personally, after jumping through a whole bunch of distros, Fedora was the best for me (it felt closest to the performance I was getting from FreeBSD while also having the newest software). OpenSuse is also an option you can try - they used to have a really stable OS.

I had a usb stick configured to boot Puppy Linux. That was always in my wallet - I'd use it to surf from school computers (I didn't trust malware on those windows PCs). I also loved Mandriva (but I don't know if they still make those anymore). Debian is great if you like a linux distro that comes built with tons and tons of software (One version I remember required 5 dvds to store the entire distro). There is also CentOS if you want stability above all else (at the cost of slightly older versions of software).

Lastly, I want to talk about Ubuntu. Ubuntu is great for beginners because of the extensive documentation in ubuntu forums. However, I got bored with Ubuntu very quickly - it wasn't good at any one thing, it just attempted to be mediocre at many things (although, it was excellent to begin with. Also, my apologies for ubuntu fans and developers - this is just my personal opinion of the ubuntu experience once ubuntu shifted to use Unity).

Your laptop should easily run the latest version of GNOME - you don't need xfce. Also, the latest GNOME versions are even better than OS X in my opinion (integration with Google Drive!!).

Finally, here's something I would only suggest to hardcore geeks - archLinux. It will teach you about your computer more than any computer science course in the world can ever manage to. You'll learn what fits where, why somethings are the way they are, you'll know more about the latest standards in software, internet technologies, what packages are available and what media standards are proprietary in a way that nothing else can compare. It's great if you are into such stuff.

Finally, check out some BSD operating systems (DragonflyBSD, FreeBSD) etc. They are excellent.

And if you are really brave, check out Debian/GNU - it's what GNU was supposed to be all along. Last I heard, around 60% of their packages were stable (this was a long long time ago).

Have fun and welcome to the world of freedom, sharing and software rights. There's no going back beyond this point :)

I recommend any of the "out of the box" distros. However, the key thing isn't really the distro (for a newb), but rather your DE, or lack of it. Some people choose distros based on the DE they come with, not realizing that they can be swapped out. Pick the wrong one, get a bad impression, and suddenly you don't like Linux anymore.

Seeing your specs, it's not worth it to run a beefier DE, like gnome, kde, unity, or cinnamon. Something like XFCE, LXDE, or even just a window manager would be much more useful. I have my dad set up with Manjaro running LXDE, and he had no problem getting used to it, coming from windows 8. I personally just run i3wm, because I like to run a bit leaner and meaner.

So, I'm gonna recommend Manjaro with LXDE. Works out of the box, has a nice lean DE, pretty newb friendly, and you'll be able to use the archwiki to solve any problem.

Also, do not be swayed by eye candy. You can make everything look pretty by yourself, so focus on functionality and ease of use as you try things out. Furthermore, expect to fuck up. Expect to distrohop. Expect to start from scratch. Embrace the learning experience, and don't be afraid of throwing it all away and starting over in these early days of experimentation. You won't be losing any data, because you don't have any on a fresh install.

Good luck, have fun, and ask questions, even the stupid ones.
